newsitem.title: UK: UK credit card data said to overstate spending.
newsitem.headline: UK credit card data said to overstate spending.

text.p: The extent of the boom in consumer spending in Britain is being over-stated because of a misunderstanding of the role of credit cards, the Credit Card Research Group (CCRG) said on Wednesday.

Announcing publication of a report entitled "Lies, Damned Lies and Credit Card Statistics," it said credit cards were firstly a means of payment and only secondly a borrowing tool. A superficial reading of Bank of England lending data could therefore be dangerously misleading.
"The consumer boom is over-rated by city commentators and economists who have misinterpreted the role played by credit cards," said the group, which represents major UK credit and debit card issuers.
"The reason why the bald gross lending statistics distort the true picture is that cards are used as a simple means of payment as well as a method of borrowing," it added.
"For example, credit card spending accounted for 55 percent of the Bank's gross unsecured lending figures in June. In reality, credit cards account for less than a quarter of unsecured borrowing."
Strong consumer spending has been the main driving force behind surging economic growth in Britain this year. Gross domestic product (GDP) grew an annual 3.4 percent in the second quarter.

Official interest rates have been raised three times in as many months to 6.75 percent to prevent a resurgence of inflation and many economists believe the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee may raise them again on Thursday after its two-day monthly meeting.

The CCRG noted that credit cards carried interest-free periods of up to 56 days and interest was not charged on more than a quarter of credit outstanding on cards. "The balance is repaid by people who only use their cards as a means of payment," the CCRG said.
Mortgages and other types of personal loans were a true record of consumer borrowing. Strong growth in both this year indicated the real rate of economic recovery, the CCRG said.
